analysis.one_liner: Taxes big oil companies' record profits and cracks down on gasoline price gouging, OPEC, and oil market speculation.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a real vote: on June 10, 2008, a move to start Senate debate failed 51-43, short of the 60 votes needed, after 41 of 49 Senate Republicans voted no.
analysis.plain_summary: In mid-2008, gas prices had doubled since 2001 to more than $3.50 a gallon, and Senate Democrats put forward a package aimed at oil companies and oil markets. It would strip a tax deduction from the biggest oil companies, charge them a 25% tax on profits above their 2002-2006 average, put that money into a fund for cheaper and cleaner energy, make gasoline price gouging during a declared energy emergency illegal, suspend government purchases of oil for the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, let US courts sue OPEC for price-fixing, and force higher trading deposits and more transparency on oil futures markets. Republicans blocked the bill from even coming up for debate.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, workers, and small businesses hit by record gasoline and heating fuel prices. The bill's stated purpose is 'energy price relief' for people paying sky-high prices [S3]. Price gouging penalties, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve suspension, and speculation limits are all aimed at lowering what drivers pay at the pump [S2]. Revenue from the oil taxes would fund programs that 'reduce the burdens on consumers of rising energy prices' and expand cheaper alternatives [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and small businesses paying record fuel prices

how_it_helps.text: Charges major oil companies (those producing at least 500,000 barrels a day) a 25% tax on profits above their reasonably inflated 2002-2006 average, unless they invest in renewable energy facilities

Makes it illegal to charge 'unconscionably excessive' gasoline or fuel prices during a President-declared energy emergency, with civil penalties up to $5 million and criminal penalties up to 5 years in prison, enforced by the FTC and state attorneys general
Suspends federal purchases of oil for the Strategic Petroleum Reserve through the end of 2008, putting more oil back into the consumer market
Allows US courts to prosecute OPEC states and other foreign oil cartels under antitrust law for limiting production or fixing prices, by removing their sovereign immunity

Directs the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to substantially raise margin (deposit) requirements for crude oil futures trades and require foreign exchanges trading US oil to publish the same position-limit and trading data as US exchanges, to curb speculation

analysis.who_pays: Major integrated oil companies, which would lose a domestic production tax deduction, face limits on foreign tax credits, and pay the windfall profits tax [S2]. Foreign oil states like OPEC members, which would face antitrust lawsuits in US courts [S2]. Oil futures traders and foreign exchanges, which would face higher margin deposits and disclosure requirements [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Big oil companies, OPEC, and futures speculators

drawbacks.text: The windfall profits tax and the loss of the domestic production deduction would raise the tax bill of the largest oil producers, and critics argued such taxes discourage domestic drilling and refining — the US imposed a similar windfall profits tax in 1980 and it was blamed for reducing domestic production and repealed in the 1990s

Raising margin levels and transparency rules for oil futures could reduce trading liquidity in the market, and a required study in the bill itself acknowledges uncertainty about how margin changes affect trade volume and volatility

The price gouging ban only applies after a presidential emergency declaration and penalties for independent small gasoline marketers are capped lower ($500,000) than for other suppliers, so ordinary stations face enforcement risk during emergencies while the main market price problem would remain untouched in normal times

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefits to consumers — anti-gouging enforcement, more oil on the market from the Reserve suspension, and pressure on speculation — are modest and situational, and the windfall tax carries a real tradeoff: taxing oil companies' profits can discourage domestic production, which economists say contributed to the repeal of the 1980s version. The strongest parts of the bill are the accountability measures — taxing profits above a historical baseline, letting courts reach OPEC, and shining light on off-shore oil trading. It is a legitimate consumer-protection package with some poorly designed pieces, and it was never allowed a full Senate debate where those design flaws could have been argued out.

outcome.mechanism: Senate Republicans filibustered the motion to even bring the bill up for debate; a cloture vote on June 10, 2008 got 51 of the 60 votes needed, and the bill never received a debate or an up-or-down vote.

narrative.text: Senator Harry Reid introduced the Consumer-First Energy Act on May 20, 2008, with 23 cosponsors (22 Democrats and 1 Independent), and it was placed on the Senate calendar the next day

Over several days in early June 2008, Majority Leader Reid repeatedly made motions to proceed to the bill and filed cloture motions — a cloture vote is the vote needed to end a filibuster and start debate, requiring 60 senators
On June 10, 2008, cloture on the motion to proceed failed 51-43: 43 of 49 Democrats and both Independents voted yes, while 41 of 49 Republicans voted no
Because the bill never got past the motion to proceed, it was never debated, amended, or voted on, and it died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The major oil companies kept the domestic production tax deduction and their record profits untaxed, OPEC kept its immunity from US antitrust suits, and oil futures traders kept the looser off-shore trading rules. The bill's backers — record gas prices were the political backdrop — gained a campaign issue instead of a law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big oil companies and futures traders

for.name: Sen. Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and, over three weeks, repeatedly moved to bring it to the floor and filed cloture motions to break the filibuster

for.name: 43 of 49 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes to cut off debate-delay and start consideration of the bill

for.name: 23 Senate cosponsors
for.role: 22 Democrats and 1 Independent cosponsoring the bill

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders and Sen. Joseph Lieberman
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on cloture on the motion to proceed

against.what_they_did: Voted no on the cloture motion, denying the 60 votes needed to begin debate on the bill

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: His administration opposed the bill and threatened a veto, pressing Senate Republicans to hold together against it

sides.party_line_note: The vote split almost entirely by party: 43 of 49 Democrats plus both Independents voted to start debate, while 41 of 49 Republicans voted no; only 6 Republicans crossed over.

industries.note: Companies producing at least 500,000 barrels a day would lose a domestic production tax deduction, face foreign tax credit limits, and pay a 25% windfall profits tax on profits above their 2002-2006 baseline. The bill existed because record prices were transferring billions from consumers to these firms, which fought to keep them.

industries.industry: Oil futures traders and foreign exchanges
industries.note: Traders in off-shore oil contracts (such as on London-based exchanges) would face substantially higher margin deposits and mandatory disclosure of speculative positions. The bill blamed 'rampant speculation' for magnifying price spikes that consumers paid at the pump.

NOPEC would strip foreign oil states of sovereign immunity and let the Attorney General sue them for production limits and price-fixing that affect US prices. OPEC governments and the oil trade depending on cartel pricing had a direct stake in stopping it.

Oil tax revenue would flow into an Energy Independence and Security Trust Fund for cleaner energy programs, and oil companies could offset windfall tax by investing in renewable facilities — a subsidy shift from oil to alternatives.

They would be subject to gouging penalties during declared emergencies, but at a lower $500,000 cap than larger suppliers, and the ban requires prices to exceed costs actually incurred, protecting marketers hit by genuine supply shocks.
